notes: For independence, integer-range-typed-value-type tests a typed bound rather than constant defaults, and channel-direction-narrowing replaces the separate buffered-drain fact; channel-range-until-close covers draining.

cards.statement: If ready's first call returns false, `for ready() { work() }` skips its body.
cards.explanation: A condition-only for loop checks ready before entering its body. A false initial result skips that body.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: A three-clause for loop accepts a short variable declaration as its post statement.
cards.explanation: Go rejects := in the post position of a three-clause for loop. An assignment or another permitted simple statement belongs there.
cards.misconception: The post statement of a three-clause for loop accepts := declarations.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, range `:=` variables get per-iteration scope by default with go.mod go 1.22 or later.
cards.explanation: Range variables declared with := belong to individual iterations when the module declares go 1.22 or later.
cards.appliesTo: Go 1.22 and later (go.mod go 1.22 or later)

source.title: Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, with go.mod go 1.22 or later, Go copies loop init `:=` variables into new ones before post by default.
cards.explanation: A three-clause loop's next declared variable starts with the previous iteration variable's current value. The post statement then operates on this new variable.
cards.appliesTo: Go 1.22 and later (go.mod go 1.22 or later)

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: With nil p of type `*struct{ A [3]int }`, the loop `for i := range p.A { _ = i }` evaluates its p.A selector.
cards.explanation: In an index-only range, constant len(p.A) makes Go skip evaluating p.A. The field selector therefore does not dereference the nil p here.
cards.misconception: Range evaluates its expression even when the index-only constant-length exception applies.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: If f returns a nil *[3]int, the loop `for i := range f() { _ = i }` runs three iterations.
cards.explanation: An index-only range over an array pointer generates indexes from the array length. It does not index the pointed-to array, so its nil pointer is safe here.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: A range loop over a nil []int slice raises a panic before its first iteration.
cards.explanation: A nil slice contributes zero entries to range, so the loop body runs zero times.
cards.misconception: A nil slice causes range to panic before iteration starts.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, ranging over a positive integer n yields integer values from 0 through n-1.
cards.explanation: An integer range uses n as an exclusive upper bound, so its last iteration value is n-1.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, `for i := range int64(3)` declares i with type int by default.
cards.explanation: Ranging over a typed integer makes the iteration variable use the bound's type. Here, int64(3) makes i an int64.
cards.misconception: Integer range declares an int iteration variable regardless of the bound's integer type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.23, a range loop's yield function panics when an iterator invokes it after it returns false.
cards.explanation: Once yield returns false, that range iteration has stopped. A later call to the same yield function panics.

source.title: iter package — Iterators

cards.statement: A `continue Outer` inside an inner loop advances that inner loop when Outer labels an enclosing outer loop.
cards.explanation: continue Outer advances the enclosing loop labeled Outer. Nested placement does not redirect it to the innermost loop.
cards.misconception: A labeled continue still targets the nearest loop surrounding the statement.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Continue statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.23, iter.Pull's stop function consumes the remaining sequence before ending iteration.
cards.explanation: iter.Pull's stop function ends iteration early. Call it when abandoning a sequence that next has yet to report as finished.
cards.misconception: Stopping a pull iterator drains its remaining sequence.

source.title: iter package — Pull

cards.statement: The Go program continues running after a panic escapes a worker goroutine.
cards.explanation: A panic that escapes a worker goroutine terminates the whole program, even when the panic originates outside main.
cards.misconception: An unrecovered panic ends the worker goroutine while leaving the rest of the Go program running.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Handling panics

cards.statement: Two `errors.New("x")` calls return error values that compare equal with `==`.
cards.explanation: errors.New creates a fresh error value for a call, so equal message text does not make separately created errors equal.
cards.misconception: Matching message text makes separately created errors the same error value.

source.title: errors package — New

cards.statement: The call `fmt.Errorf("read: %v", err)` wraps the error supplied as `err`.
cards.explanation: In fmt.Errorf, %v adds an error's text; %w records the supplied error as a wrapped operand.
cards.misconception: Formatting an error with %v preserves it as a wrapped error.

source.title: fmt package — Errorf

cards.statement: With two error operands, `fmt.Errorf("%w; %w", a, b)` returns an error with `Unwrap() []error`.
cards.explanation: fmt.Errorf with several %w verbs returns an error whose Unwrap method returns the wrapped operands as []error.

source.title: fmt package — Errorf

cards.statement: For an error tree, `errors.Is` checks the root before descending depth-first through its children.
cards.explanation: errors.Is explores one child branch depth-first before checking a sibling branch, after checking the current error.

source.title: errors package — Is

cards.statement: The call `errors.As(errors.New("x"), nil)` raises a run-time panic.
cards.explanation: errors.As needs a non-nil target pointer to an error type or interface. Passing nil for the target with a real error triggers a panic.

source.title: errors package — As

cards.statement: Since Go 1.26, `errors.AsType` reports a failed type search with a panic by default.
cards.explanation: When errors.AsType[E] finds no matching error, it returns E's zero value and false.
cards.misconception: errors.AsType treats an unsuccessful type match as a run-time panic.

source.title: errors package — AsType

cards.statement: Calling `errors.Join` with two nil error arguments produces a nil `error` result.
cards.explanation: errors.Join discards nil arguments; an input list containing only nil values leaves it with no errors to join.

source.title: errors package — Join

cards.statement: Calling `errors.Unwrap` on an error returned by `errors.Join` returns its first wrapped error.
cards.explanation: errors.Unwrap calls Unwrap() error. A non-nil joined error exposes Unwrap() []error, so errors.Unwrap returns nil for it.
cards.misconception: errors.Unwrap extracts the first child from an error that wraps several errors.

source.title: errors package — Unwrap

cards.statement: A panic runs the deferred calls on the panicking goroutine's call stack as it unwinds.
cards.explanation: During a panic, Go executes the deferred calls belonging to functions affected on that goroutine's stack.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Handling panics

cards.statement: After completed recovery in its deferred function, the enclosing function continues after the panicking call.
cards.explanation: A function containing a recovery defer returns to its caller when recovery completes successfully; its body does not resume at the panic site.
cards.misconception: Recovery resumes the enclosing function's ordinary body immediately after the call that panicked.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Handling panics

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, `panic(nil)` produces a `*runtime.PanicNilError` panic value by default.
cards.explanation: Go supplies a *runtime.PanicNilError as the panic value, so a valid recover call receives an error value.

source.title: runtime package — PanicNilError

cards.statement: In `go f(g())`, the calling goroutine evaluates g() before f starts in the new goroutine.
cards.explanation: A go statement evaluates and saves the call's arguments in the calling goroutine before starting the invoked function.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Go statements

cards.statement: When main returns, Go keeps the program running until its other goroutines finish.
cards.explanation: Returning from main ends the program. Remaining goroutines do not keep it alive.
cards.misconception: Remaining goroutines keep a Go program alive after main returns.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Program execution

cards.statement: A send on an unbuffered channel completes before a matching receive becomes ready.
cards.explanation: An unbuffered send proceeds when a matching receiver is ready to communicate.
cards.misconception: An unbuffered send finishes before its receiving operation becomes ready.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Send statements

cards.statement: A send on an open buffered channel proceeds when its buffer has room for the sent value.
cards.explanation: A buffered send needs space in the channel buffer. The channel accepts the value into its available buffer space.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Send statements

cards.statement: Receiving from a nil channel immediately yields the zero value of its element type.
cards.explanation: A receive from a nil channel blocks forever. The operation has no communication that could make it proceed.
cards.misconception: A nil channel immediately supplies a zero value to a receiver.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Receive operator

cards.statement: A function parameter of type `<-chan int` accepts an argument of type `chan int`.
cards.explanation: Assigning a bidirectional channel to a receive-only channel type narrows the operations permitted through that parameter.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Assignability

cards.statement: Sending a value on a closed channel raises a run-time panic, even if its buffer has free space.
cards.explanation: Closing a channel ends its sending phase. A later send triggers a panic instead of storing the value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Send statements

cards.statement: The call `close(ch)` type-checks for a parameter ch declared as `<-chan int`.
cards.explanation: close requires a channel whose type permits sends. A receive-only <-chan int channel is rejected at compile time.
cards.misconception: A receive-only channel parameter permits its receiver to close the channel.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Close

cards.statement: The loop `for range ch {}` ends when it receives from ch after closure and after ch's buffer drains.
cards.explanation: The loop receives values until closure and exhaustion of the channel's buffer. An empty open channel makes this loop wait for another value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — For statements

cards.statement: By default, a select with several ready communication cases chooses the one appearing first in source order.
cards.explanation: select chooses among ready communication cases by uniform pseudo-random selection. Source order provides no priority.
cards.misconception: select chooses its first ready case in source order.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Select statements

cards.statement: A select executes its default branch while its communication cases are blocked.
cards.explanation: The default branch gives select a path to proceed when no channel communication is ready.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Select statements

cards.statement: The expression `len(ch)` reports the number of free buffer slots in a buffered channel ch.
cards.explanation: len(ch) counts values queued in the channel buffer. Free slots are the buffer capacity minus that count.
cards.misconception: The length of a channel measures its unused buffer capacity.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Length and capacity

cards.statement: Go's memory model gives data-race-free programs sequentially consistent behavior.
cards.explanation: A race-free Go program's outcomes match an interleaving of goroutine operations that preserves each goroutine's program order.

source.title: The Go Memory Model

cards.statement: Go preserves slice descriptor consistency during concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes.
cards.explanation: A race on a multiword slice value can expose components from different writes. Such inconsistent pointer and length pairs can cause memory corruption.
cards.misconception: Go preserves the internal consistency of slice values even when goroutines race on them.

source.title: The Go Memory Model

cards.statement: Unlocking a used `sync.Mutex` makes subsequent copies of that mutex safe for synchronization.
cards.explanation: The sync contract prohibits copying a Mutex after its first use; unlocking it does not reset that restriction.
cards.misconception: An unlocked Mutex becomes safe to copy even after earlier use.

source.title: sync package — Mutex

cards.statement: A locked `sync.Mutex` accepts `Unlock` from a goroutine other than the one that locked it.
cards.explanation: A Mutex has no goroutine owner. One goroutine can lock it and arrange for another goroutine to unlock the same mutex.

source.title: sync package — Mutex.Unlock

cards.statement: Calling `sync.RWMutex.Lock` while holding its read lock upgrades that lock to a write lock.
cards.explanation: RWMutex offers no read-to-write lock upgrade. Lock waits for outstanding readers, including the caller's own read lock, to release their locks.
cards.misconception: Calling Lock converts an existing RWMutex read lock into a write lock.

source.title: sync package — RWMutex

cards.statement: Since Go 1.25, `sync.WaitGroup.Go` tracks its function as a task until that function returns.
cards.explanation: WaitGroup.Go adds the function's task to the group and removes it on return, so Wait includes that task.

source.title: sync package — WaitGroup.Go

cards.statement: A `sync.Once` treats a panic from the function passed to `Do` as a completed invocation.
cards.explanation: If the function passed to Once.Do panics, later Do calls on that Once return without invoking the function again.

source.title: sync package — Once.Do

cards.statement: The `atomic.Int64.Swap` method returns the new value that it stores in the variable.
cards.explanation: atomic.Int64.Swap replaces the stored value atomically and returns the value present before the swap.
cards.misconception: Swap reports the newly stored value instead of the preceding value.

source.title: sync/atomic package — Int64.Swap

cards.statement: Calling a child context's cancel function also cancels the parent context it derives from.
cards.explanation: Calling the cancel function returned for a child context affects that child's cancellation; it leaves the parent's cancellation state unchanged.
cards.misconception: Cancellation of a derived context propagates upward to its parent.

source.title: context package — Cancellation

cards.statement: A caller releases a derived context's cancellation resources by invoking its CancelFunc.
cards.explanation: Calling the CancelFunc removes the parent's reference to the child context and stops associated timers.

source.title: context package — Cancellation

cards.statement: After its cancel function records a `*MyError` cause, a `context.WithCancelCause` context returns it from `Err`.
cards.explanation: Context.Err reports context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded. context.Cause retrieves a separately recorded custom cancellation error.
cards.misconception: A custom cancellation cause replaces the standard error returned by Context.Err.

source.title: context package — WithCancelCause

cards.statement: When `context.AfterFunc` invokes its callback after cancellation, the callback runs in its own goroutine.
cards.explanation: The callback runs in a separate goroutine, including when the context is already canceled at registration.

source.title: context package — AfterFunc
